families.s: HSE whole-body-vibration and mobile-machine back-risk guidance
families.t: vehicle selection, routes, seats, speed, maintenance, exposure action and limit values and combined back-risk controls
f: Whole-body vibration mainly affects drivers of off-road vehicles such as dumpers, excavators and agricultural tractors.
It can also affect some vehicles used on paved surfaces or rails.
Whole-body vibration and shocks are transmitted through seats or standing surfaces when vehicles travel over rough ground or tracks.
Low-level exposure alone is unlikely to cause back pain but can aggravate existing back injury.
The whole-body-vibration exposure action value is 0.5 m/s² A(8).
The whole-body-vibration exposure limit value is 1.15 m/s² A(8).
Controls include suitable vehicles, maintained routes, adjusted suspension seats, appropriate speed and reduced exposure duration.
Other causes of back pain, including manual handling and poor posture, must also be assessed and controlled.
families.g: WBV risk depends on vibration and shock magnitude, exposure duration, vehicle and seat, route roughness, speed, posture, manual handling, maintenance, existing back conditions and work organisation.

families.s: HSE occupational heat-stress assessment and control guidance
families.t: metabolic heat, climate, clothing, PPE, acclimatisation, symptoms, hydration, exposure time and emergency response
f: Heat stress occurs when the body's mechanisms for controlling internal temperature begin to fail.
Risk is influenced by work rate, air temperature, humidity, air movement and work clothing or PPE.
Symptoms can include poor concentration, cramps, rash, severe thirst, fainting and heat exhaustion.
Heat stroke can cause hot dry skin, confusion, convulsions, unconsciousness and death if not detected early.
Employers must assess heat-stress risk where it may occur and consult workers about early signs.
Controls include reducing heat sources, engineering cooling, physical barriers and process changes.
Exposure can be controlled through cooler scheduling, work-rest regimes, reduced work rate, mechanical aids and recovery areas.
Heavy or impermeable PPE can prevent sweat evaporation and increase body-heat load.
families.g: Heat-stress risk depends on metabolic work rate, air and radiant temperature, humidity, air movement, clothing and PPE, hydration, acclimatisation, medication, health and exposure duration.

families.t: reasonable indoor temperature, environmental and personal factors, local heating or cooling, ventilation, breaks and worker consultation
f: There is no statutory maximum workplace temperature because workplaces and processes differ.
Indoor workrooms should normally be at least 16°C or 13°C where work involves rigorous physical effort.
Air temperature alone is not a sufficient indicator of thermal comfort or heat stress.
Thermal comfort depends on air temperature, radiant temperature, air movement, humidity, clothing or PPE and work rate.
Employers should provide a reasonable working temperature and local heating or cooling where whole-room comfort cannot be maintained.
Systems may include ventilation, fans, blinds, insulation, flexible hours, job rotation and suitable recovery breaks.
PPE selection and work systems should account for retained heat and restricted sweat evaporation.
Workers should report uncomfortable temperatures so risks can be reassessed and controls agreed and reviewed.
families.g: Thermal comfort depends on combined environmental and personal factors, process heat or cold, clothing, work intensity, individual health, building performance, duration and local control options.

families.s: HSE occupational-contact-dermatitis prevention and surveillance guidance
families.t: irritant and allergic dermatitis, wet work, sensitisation, substitution, skin protection, symptom reporting and surveillance
f: Dermatitis can result from contact with an irritant or from an allergic reaction to a sensitising substance.
Signs can include redness, scaling, blistering, weeping, cracking and swelling, with itching or pain.
Repeated wet work, soaps, detergents, solvents, oils, dust, acids, alkalis and wet cement can cause irritant dermatitis.
Allergic contact dermatitis can recur after very small exposures once a worker has become sensitised.
Healthcare employers should assess irritant and allergic contact-dermatitis risks from wet work, chemicals and biological or physical agents.
Food and catering work commonly involves dermatitis risks from water, soaps, detergents and contact with foods.
Where residual risk remains and disease is reasonably foreseeable, health surveillance can detect early skin changes.
A trained responsible person may perform regular visual skin checks and refer abnormalities for competent occupational-health review.
families.g: Dermatitis risk depends on substance and sensitising potential, concentration, wet-work duration, skin condition, contact frequency, glove suitability, hygiene, individual susceptibility and surveillance.

families.s: HSE welding-fume cancer, respiratory-risk and exposure-control guidance
families.t: substitution, process selection, mechanisation, LEV, RPE, ventilation, maintenance, training and health surveillance
f: Employers must control health risks from welding fume for specialist and occasional welding work.
All welding fume can cause lung cancer and can also cause occupational asthma and other disease.
Welding fume is controlled under COSHH.
The control hierarchy starts with avoiding or reducing fume generation before using extraction and respiratory protection.
Alternative joining methods, mechanisation, automation and lower-fume welding processes can reduce exposure.
Local exhaust ventilation should capture welding fume at source where reasonably practicable.
Suitable RPE is required where extraction alone does not adequately control inhalation exposure.
Welding fume can cause acute airway irritation, metal-fume illness and serious asphyxiation risk in confined spaces.
families.g: Welding-fume risk depends on process, consumables and parent metal, coatings, current and duty cycle, enclosure, ventilation, welder position, LEV capture, RPE fit and maintenance.

families.t: RCS generation, elimination, wet methods, extraction, RPE, cleaning, exposure assessment and silicosis surveillance
f: Silica occurs naturally in rock, sand and clay and in products such as concrete and bricks.
Cutting, sanding, carving and similar work can generate respirable crystalline silica dust.
RCS particles are fine enough to penetrate deep into the lungs and may be invisible in normal lighting.
Exposure can cause serious lung disease and should be prevented or adequately controlled.
Heavy and prolonged RCS exposure has the potential to cause lung cancer.
Health surveillance for silicosis should be considered for high-risk construction, foundry, ceramics, quarry and stone work.
Where workers are regularly exposed and silicosis is reasonably likely, health surveillance must be provided.
Workers and employers should use effective dust controls and safe methods rather than relying on visible dust as an indicator.
families.g: RCS risk depends on silica content, process energy, dustiness, duration, enclosure, wet suppression, extraction, housekeeping, RPE, worker location and actual airborne exposure.

families.s: HSE occupational-lead exposure, control and medical-surveillance guidance
families.t: lead identification, inhalation and ingestion control, hygiene, air monitoring, biological monitoring, medical surveillance and worker protection
f: The Control of Lead at Work Regulations require employers to prevent or, where prevention is not reasonably practicable, control exposure to lead.
The regulations apply to inhalable lead dust, vapour or fume, ingestible lead powder, dust, paint or paste and specified skin-absorbable compounds.
Lead exposure can affect blood, the nervous system, kidneys, blood pressure and reproductive function.
Construction exposure can arise from lead sheet, old leaded paint, pipework and dust or fume from disturbing lead-containing materials.
Employers should identify lead tasks, assess significant exposure, control the process and review the controls.
The occupational exposure limit for lead in air is specified in the Control of Lead at Work Regulations.
Blood-lead monitoring and suspension levels form part of statutory medical surveillance for relevant workers.
Lead controls must cover handling, processing, maintenance, storage, cleaning and disposal activities that can expose workers or others.
families.g: Lead risk depends on chemical form, airborne and surface contamination, task and temperature, ingestion controls, hygiene, RPE, duration, worker age and reproductive status, monitoring and medical surveillance.

families.s: HSE wood-dust asthma, cancer, dermatitis and extraction guidance
families.t: hardwood and softwood dust, source extraction, RPE, cleaning, exposure control and health surveillance
f: Wood dust can cause occupational asthma and may also cause dermatitis and irritation of the respiratory tract and eyes.
Hardwood dust can cause a rare form of nasal cancer.
COSHH requires hazardous-substance exposure to be prevented or adequately controlled.
Dust extraction should control wood dust at woodworking processes.
Vacuum cleaning equipment should be suitable for the dust hazard rather than dispersing dust through dry sweeping or compressed air.
Many machining and short-duration dusty tasks require suitable respiratory protection in addition to extraction.
Higher-risk woods that can cause asthma should be substituted where reasonably practicable.
Health surveillance supports early detection of asthma or dermatitis but does not replace exposure control.
families.g: Wood-dust risk depends on species and material, process, dust generation, extraction capture, enclosure, cleaning method, RPE, duration, sensitisation and health-surveillance findings.
